name: Sorbung
confidence_why: One first-hand description, checked against the source.
catalog_citation: Mortensen, David & Jennifer Keogh. 2011. Sorbung, an undocumented language of Manipur: its phonology and place in Tibeto-Burman. Journal of the Southeast Asian Linguistics Society (JSEALS) 4(1): 64-114.
catalog_locator: sec. 2.1 Stress, pp. 73-75 (full PDF of JSEALS 4(1) via the Internet Archive jseals.org/, saved our source folder/)
catalog_quote: All of these correlates point to a general iambic pattern of stress. This is not to say, however, that Sorbung stress is predictable without reference to morphological structure. The following general principles seem to hold: 1. Minor syllables are never stressed. This may be due to the fact that the vowels in these syllables are epenthetic. 2. The last root syllable in a compound stem, not counting derivational suffixes, is stressed. 3. Two consecutive unstressed syllables are not tolerated. 4. Stress assignment is cyclic. ‘Underarm hair,’ from the compound cubˈlaa (cuup ‘breast’ plus laa ‘crotch’) plus míi ‘hair’ is cubˌlaaˈmíi rather than *ˌcuublaˈmíi. 5. Suffixes do not affect the stress of the base to which they are attached: ˈlook ‘big’, ˈloog-ˌoo ‘big-DECL’, ʔˈʉʉ ‘dog’, ʔˈʉʉ-e ‘dog-NOM’. 6. tone_statements.citation: Lotven, Samson. 2023. Tone in South Central Tibeto-Burman. Himalayan Linguistics 22(1): 36-66. (Special issue on Kuki-Chin / South Central.)
tone_statements.quote: For example, Lemi minor syllables do not exhibit a tonal contrast and are realized with default mid pitch (Herr 2011: 58); and while Sorbung’s major syllables contrast L, M, and H tone, minor syllable tone is dependent on phonological context (Mortensen and Keogh 2011: 79-82). ... Sorbung offers evidence of a general dissimilation rule, where a sequence of two adjacent smooth syllables with H tone (/H-H/) is realized as [H-M] (Mortensen and Keogh 2011).
tone_statements.locator: p. 45, sec. 5.1 'Minor syllable tone'; p. 51, sec. 6 (tone rules: dissimilation); summary p. 46 sec. 5.3
tone_statements.summary: Three contrastive tones (Low, Mid, High) on major (full) syllables; minor (reduced) syllables have no independent tone, their pitch determined by context; tone sandhi: /H-H/ on adjacent smooth syllables surfaces as [H-M] (dissimilation). Nothing said about stress or its interaction with tone (all per M&K 2011).

tone_statements.quote: 2.4 TONE Kaprang-Tangkul has two tones. They are level and falling tone (level tone is not marked here and falling tone is marked as ( ̀ ). These, two tones can be established by the minimal pairs as given below: Level tone ... Falling tone / sa ‘eat’ sà ‘animal’ / insa ‘drink’ insà ‘domestic animal’ / pa ‘read’ pà ‘father’ / pi ‘give’ pì ‘grand mother’ / mai ‘face’ maì ‘pumpkin’ / aci ‘egg’ acì ‘sweet snack’
tone_statements.locator: Ch. II Phonology, section 2.4 Tone, p. 35; restated in the Conclusion chapter: 'And 2 (two) suprasegmentals phoneme are level and falling tones.'
tone_statements.summary: Kabrang (Kaprang) Tangkhul: two tones, level vs falling, shown by six minimal pairs; grave accent marks falling. Half-page section; nothing on TBU, sandhi or stress.

audit.reasoning: Quote check: all three quoted passages (deciding, domain, exception) found verbatim in the held JSEALS 4(1) PDF at the stated section and pages. Deciding source: a 2011 peer-reviewed phonological description from primary fieldwork, the only description of Sorbung in existence (Glottolog: 3 refs total, the other two being an 1837 one-page vocabulary and a 2014 PhD on a different, neighbouring lect). The classification 'morphological' (last root syllable of stem stressed, suffixes stress-neutral or lexically stressed/unstressed, cyclic, iambic/right-headed) is a faithful reading of the source's seven principles. No better or newer stress source exists; web checks (Glottolog languoid + reference records, Crossref) surfaced nothing further
